# Dimensionality and local independence {#dimensionality}

<div class="goals">
**Learning goals.** After this chapter you can

* explain the assumptions of unidimensionality and local independence;
* compare one- and two-factor models and read rotated factor loadings;
* fit a confirmatory model in which each item measures a named dimension;
* read standardized residuals and Yen's Q3, and tell local dependence from a
  second trait;
* choose a remedy for locally dependent items.
</div>

**Key terms:**
[dimensionality](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#dimensionality),
[local independence](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#local-independence),
[local dependence](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#local-dependence),
[Q3](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#q3),
[multidimensional IRT](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#multidimensional-irt).

## The ideas

The models in Chapter \@ref(irt-models) make two related assumptions.
**Unidimensionality** says that one latent trait accounts for the
relationships among the items. **Local independence** says that once we know
a person's $\theta$, their responses to different items are independent: the
only reason two items correlate is that both depend on $\theta$.

Both can fail, in different ways.

* A test may measure **two or more traits**, for example reading and
  arithmetic in a set of mathematics word problems. Then a one-factor model
  forces two traits into one score, and the items of the smaller dimension
  look poorly discriminating.
* A **small cluster of items** may share something beyond the trait: a
  common reading passage, a shared stimulus, near-identical wording, or an
  item whose answer gives away the next. These pairs or clusters are *locally
  dependent*. They look like extra-good items, they inflate reliability, and
  they distort the item parameters.

The tools differ too. For the first problem we compare models with one and
two factors and look at the factor loadings. For the second we look at what
is left over after fitting a one-factor model: if local independence holds,
the residual correlations between item pairs should be close to zero. Yen's
**Q3** statistic [@yen1984] is the correlation between two items' residuals.
Values well above the average Q3 (often by 0.2 or more) flag dependent pairs.

## Example 1: a mathematics test with a reading dimension

We simulate a 24-item mathematics test taken by 1,500 Grade 8 students.
Items M01 to M12 are calculation items. Items W01 to W12 are word problems
that also depend on reading, which correlates 0.5 with calculation skill.

```{r data-dimensionality-1}
# Simulated 24-item test, two correlated traits (r = 0.5), 12 items each.
set.seed(404)
a <- cbind(c(runif(12, 1.0, 2.0), runif(12, 0.3, 0.6)),
           c(rep(0, 12),          runif(12, 1.0, 1.8)))
d <- matrix(rnorm(24, 0, 0.8))
sigma <- matrix(c(1, 0.5, 0.5, 1), 2)
resp <- simdata(a, d, N = 1500, itemtype = "2PL", sigma = sigma)
colnames(resp) <- c(sprintf("M%02d", 1:12), sprintf("W%02d", 1:12))
```

First, an exploratory comparison of one and two factors. We keep a copy of
the data as `math` for the exercises.

```{r}
math <- resp
f1 <- mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE)
f2 <- mirt(resp, 2, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE)
anova(f1, f2)
```

The two-factor model is far better on every criterion. `summary()` shows the
standardized loadings after an oblique rotation, which lets the factors
correlate:

```{r}
summary(f2, rotate = "oblimin", suppress = 0.25)
```

The calculation items load on one factor and the word problems on the
other. The factor correlation is higher than the 0.5 we simulated between
the two traits, because the word problems also need calculation skill: the
rotation cannot separate that shared part cleanly, so some of it shows up as
correlation between the factors. The one-factor fit statistics give the same
message from the other side:

```{r}
rbind(one_factor = glance(f1)[, c("RMSEA", "SRMSR", "CFI")],
      two_factor = glance(f2)[, c("RMSEA", "SRMSR", "CFI")])
```

Exploratory models are useful for finding structure. When the structure is
known from the test blueprint, a **confirmatory** model states it directly.
Each item loads only on its own factor, and the factor correlation is
estimated (`COV = F1*F2`):

```{r}
spec <- mirt.model("Calc    = 1-12
                    Reading = 13-24
                    COV     = Calc*Reading")
cfa <- mirt(resp, spec, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE)
coef(cfa, simplify = TRUE)$cov
anova(cfa, f2)
```

The confirmatory model is nearly as good as the exploratory one with far
fewer parameters, so BIC prefers it. What should we report to the school?
That depends on use. Two subscores are defensible if each is reliable
enough (Chapter \@ref(information)); a single total score mixes two skills,
and students with weak reading will look weaker at mathematics than they are.

## Example 2: a reading passage that ties four items together

In this test of 20 items, items R05 to R08 all refer to the same passage.
Students who happen to understand the passage well do better on all four
than their general reading ability predicts. We simulate this with a small
extra factor that only those four items share.

```{r data-dimensionality-2}
# Simulated 20-item reading test; R05-R08 share a passage (testlet effect).
set.seed(405)
a_gen <- runif(20, 1.0, 1.8)
a_pas <- c(rep(0, 4), rep(2.0, 4), rep(0, 12))
resp <- simdata(cbind(a_gen, a_pas), matrix(rnorm(20, 0, 0.7)),
                N = 1200, itemtype = "2PL")
colnames(resp) <- sprintf("R%02d", 1:20)
```

We fit an ordinary unidimensional 2PL, as an analyst who did not know about
the passage would, and look at the Q3 matrix.

```{r q3-passage, fig.height = 5.5, fig.width = 6.5, out.width = "75%", fig.cap = "Q3 residual correlations from a unidimensional 2PL fitted to the reading test with a four-item passage."}
uni <- mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE)
gg_q3(uni)
```

The six pairs among R05 to R08 stand out. Most other Q3 values are slightly
negative, which is normal: residuals are a little negatively correlated on
average, so we judge a pair against the average Q3 rather than against zero.
The numbers behind the plot:

```{r}
q3 <- residuals(uni, type = "Q3", verbose = FALSE)
round(q3[5:8, 5:8], 2)
```

Local dependence has a cost. The unidimensional model has nowhere to put the
passage effect, so it bends the item parameters to accommodate it and treats
part of the passage effect as reading ability. Remedy 1 below shows how
different the passage items look once the dependence is modelled.

There are three common remedies.

1. **Model the dependence.** A *testlet* or *bifactor* model gives the
   passage items a specific factor of their own, uncorrelated with the
   general factor. `bfactor()` fits it; its second argument says which
   specific factor each item belongs to (`NA` for none).

```{r}
specific <- c(rep(NA, 4), rep(1, 4), rep(NA, 12))
bf <- bfactor(resp, specific, verbose = FALSE)
anova(uni, bf)
round(coef(bf, simplify = TRUE)$items[3:10, c("a1", "a2")], 2)
```

   The passage effect now has its own slope (`a2`), and the general slopes
   (`a1`) of R05 to R08 are higher than in the unidimensional model, which
   had diluted them. Compare them with
   `coef(uni, simplify = TRUE)$items[5:8, "a1"]`. Likelihood-ratio test and
   BIC both favour the bifactor model.

2. **Combine the items.** Sum R05 to R08 into one polytomous "super-item"
   scored 0 to 4 and fit a polytomous model (Chapter \@ref(polytomous)). This
   is simple and robust, at the cost of some information.

3. **Drop or rewrite items** in a future form, so that no two items depend on
   each other beyond the trait.

## Your turn

<div class="yourturn">
1. In Example 1, compute the sum score of the word problems and of the
   calculation items separately. How strongly do they correlate? Why is this
   lower than the factor correlation?
2. Use `select_model(resp, dims = 1:2)` on the data of Example 1. Which model
   does it choose?
3. In Example 2, compare the empirical reliability of the scores
   (`empirical_rxx()` on `fscores(..., full.scores.SE = TRUE)`) from the
   unidimensional model with that of the general factor of the bifactor model.
   Which one would you report, and why?
4. Make the super-item from R05 to R08, fit a graded model to the 17 items,
   and check the Q3 matrix again.
</div>

<details><summary>Solutions</summary>

```{r}
cor(rowSums(math[, 1:12]), rowSums(math[, 13:24]))
```

1. Sum scores contain measurement error, which attenuates (weakens) the
   correlation; the factor correlation is corrected for it.
```{r}
select_model(math, dims = 1:2, verbose = FALSE)
```

2. It fits one- and two-factor versions of each candidate and should prefer a
   two-factor model, because the second dimension is strong.
```{r}
empirical_rxx(fscores(uni, full.scores.SE = TRUE))
empirical_rxx(fscores(bf, full.scores.SE = TRUE))
```

3. The unidimensional model reports a somewhat higher reliability, because it
   counts the shared passage effect as signal about reading. The general
   factor of the bifactor model gives the more honest figure. With one small
   passage the difference is modest; with several passages it grows.

```{r}
super <- data.frame(resp[, -(5:8)], R05_08 = rowSums(resp[, 5:8]))
sup <- mirt(super, 1, itemtype = c(rep("2PL", 16), "graded"), verbose = FALSE)
q3s <- residuals(sup, type = "Q3", verbose = FALSE)
max(abs(q3s[upper.tri(q3s)]))
```

4. The super-item removes the dependent pairs, and the largest remaining Q3
   is small.

</details>

local dependence screen on a certification exam. Decide for yourself whether
anything needs fixing before you choose a model.

## Further reading {-}

Yen [-@yen1984] introduced Q3 and showed how local dependence affects
parameter estimates and equating. Embretson and Reise [-@embretson2000]
cover multidimensional and bifactor models.
